_readme: Grounded cultural canon. Every entry is a claim the shipped clues rest on, checked against sources. Populated from docs/research/*.md; see docs/research/CANON.md for the contract and scripts/canon.mjs to query it. Entries are keyed to specific clues, and `npm test` fails if a keyed clue no longer exists — so editing a clue out from under its citation is caught rather than silently orphaning the research.

entries.claim: The conk was a lye-based hair straightening process (congolene: lye, egg, potato) dominant from roughly the 1920s to the 1960s, and it burned.
entries.detail: Malcolm X describes his first conk in Roxbury around 1941 at age sixteen, and concludes it was "my first really big step toward self-degradation". The process was displaced by the Afro during the 1960s. The chemistry and the chronology are settled; the TONE question the bench asked is not — see shop-conk-tone.

sources.title: Byrd & Tharps, Hair Story: Untangling the Roots of Black Hair in America
Quincy T. Mills, Cutting Along the Color Line (Penn Press, 2013)

entries.claim: Whether the conk clue reads as respect for the old heads or as novelty at their expense.
entries.detail: Not answerable from sources, and research does not settle it. Malcolm X’s own conclusion was that the conk was self-degradation, so a clue treating it as period colour is standing on top of that judgement whether it means to or not. Needs a reader old enough to have had one.

entries.claim: The Black barbershop is a documented institution of Black public life, not just a business.
entries.detail: Mills inverts the assumption usefully: in the 19th century Black barbers largely served white-only clienteles by custom, and the Black room as a Black space was won after 1890. Harris-Perry treats it as a site of everyday political talk.

sources.title: Quincy T. Mills, Cutting Along the Color Line (Penn Press, 2013)
Melissa Harris-Perry, Barbershops, Bibles, and BET (Princeton, 2004)

entries.claim: Clipper guard numbers are standardised across brands; a #2 is a quarter inch.
entries.detail: Fade vs taper and line-up/edge-up are used in the packs the way barbers use them. One piece of vocabulary the packs do not use and could: the taper lever, around a sixteenth of an inch.

sources.title: Clipper guard sizes chart

entries.claim: A stylist commonly rents her own chair, paying the shop owner as a landlord rather than working for wages.
entries.detail: Booth renters are 1099 independent contractors. The pack’s "two hundred a week" sits mid-range against a sourced $150-300/week. The alternative model is commission, typically a 40-60% split.

sources.title: Employee vs booth renter vs independent contractor in the salon industry

entries.claim: A Dominican blowout takes about ninety minutes and costs around twenty-five dollars.
entries.detail: The shipped clue read "where a blowout runs an hour and costs less" — an hour understates the sourced figure of roughly ninety minutes, and "costs less" was doing the work a number does better.

sources.title: The Dominican blowout, explained

replacement.clue: The Dominican shop two blocks over: walk in, ninety minutes, out for twenty-five dollars.

entries.claim: Wash day is a multi-hour ritual, not a wash.
entries.detail: Sourced wash range is 30-90 minutes for the washing itself; the pack’s "ten until noon" describes the full wash-and-style, which is how the sources use the term. Imprecise rather than wrong.

sources.title: CNN — wash day, photographed
Byrd & Tharps, Hair Story: Untangling the Roots of Black Hair in America

entries.claim: The CROWN Act bans natural-hair discrimination. California was first, 3 July 2019. It is NOT federal law.
entries.detail: The House passed it 235-189; it never cleared the Senate. Reintroduced 26 February 2025 as H.R. 1638 / S. 751. Roughly 30 states have adopted a version. NOTE FOR AUTHORS: never put the state count in a clue — it goes stale and the clue becomes wrong without anyone touching it.

sources.title: The CROWN Act — official campaign site
NAACP Legal Defense Fund — natural hair discrimination
Jackson Lewis — House passes the CROWN Act

entries.claim: Cosmetology and barber licensing has a race history, and braiding licensure is its live continuation.
entries.detail: Braiding was licensure-regulated in 24 states as of 2014; Utah’s scheme was struck down in 2012 as "wholly irrational". This links the salon’s ownership spine to the barbershop’s licensing history — the same regulatory weapon, aimed at women, still in use.

sources.title: Regulating Beauty: The Licensing of Barbers and Beauticians in Alabama and the Nation (Enterprise & Society, Cambridge)
Institute for Justice — hair braiding licensure litigation
NPR — It’s Now Legal To Braid Hair In Utah Without A License (2012)

entries.claim: The beauty shop is a documented site of Black women’s economic independence, via Madam C.J. Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone.
entries.detail: Neither Walker nor Malone is named anywhere in the shipped salon pack. See shop-missing-beauty-shop-politics for why that absence costs the pack its strongest material.

sources.title: Library of Congress — Madam C.J. Walker
Tiffany M. Gill, Beauty Shop Politics (Univ. of Illinois Press, 2010)

entries.claim: The salon pack has practice but no political history — the single largest gap found in either pack.
entries.detail: Gill’s Beauty Shop Politics documents the beauty shop as a civil-rights organising site. Bernice Robinson, a 41-year-old Charleston beautician, taught Highlander’s first Citizenship School, and women were prepared for literacy tests in her shop at night — precisely BECAUSE a beautician’s income came from Black clients, so white employers had no economic leverage over her. That is the salon’s answer to the barbershop’s institutional weight, and the pack does not have it.

sources.title: Tiffany M. Gill, Beauty Shop Politics (Univ. of Illinois Press, 2010)
Interview: Tiffany Gill on beauty shops as a birthplace of activism (UT Austin)

entries.claim: The barbershop clue "The old word for the cut, still used here" names no actual word.
entries.detail: Barber trade glossaries and regional vocabulary searched; nothing anchors it, because there is nothing to anchor — the clue asserts a term exists without naming it. Either name the word or accept it as pure atmosphere resting on nothing.

sources.title: Clipper guard sizes chart

entries.claim: General Order No. 3 is four sentences.
entries.detail: Two shipped clues said five — the most-repeated factual error in the pack, and it sat in its most quotable clue. The National Archives text runs four: all slaves are free; absolute equality of personal rights; freedmen advised to remain and work for wages; not to collect at military posts. Some renderings collapse it to three. Nobody counts five.

sources.title: National Archives — General Order No. 3, the original document

replacement.clue: How the order goes: four sentences, the plainest language the government ever managed.

entries.claim: Emancipation Park, Houston: ten acres bought in 1872 for $800 by nine trustees; the city took title in 1916.
entries.detail: The shipped clue said "four men". The four-name short form (Allen, Brock, Yates, Dibble) describes the leadership, not the purchasers; the marker names nine trustees of the Colored People of Harris County Festival Association buying for a subscribing community. The pack’s own `parked` clue already said "freedmen", so the two clues contradicted each other.

sources.title: Historical Marker Database — The Legacy of Emancipation Park

replacement.clue: Ten acres of it in Houston, 1872, bought by nine trustees for eight hundred dollars.

entries.claim: The first public observance of the anniversary was in 1866, in Houston.
entries.detail: The shipped clue called 1866 "the second one". 19 June 1865 was the day of the order, not a celebration of it. The 1866 observance was a parade led by Elias Dibble as president and Sandy Parker as marshal. Off by one, in a way a Texas reader catches immediately.

sources.title: Britannica — Juneteenth
Rice University historian on the 1866 Houston observance (KXAN)

replacement.clue: What it took to hold the very first one in 1866, in a state that had lost and was not sorry.

entries.claim: Houston renamed Dowling Street to Emancipation Avenue in January 2017.
entries.detail: The shipped clue said the neighbourhood fought to "restore" the name. The street never carried it — it was named for Confederate commander Richard "Dick" Dowling, and the change, led by Rep. Garnet Coleman, was won rather than restored. Timed to Juneteenth 2017 and the park’s $33m reopening.

sources.title: City of Houston — Dowling Street renamed to Emancipation Avenue
Houston Public Media — Dowling Street to be renamed (Jan 2017)

replacement.clue: Emancipation, in Houston: the street the parade uses, and a Confederate's name taken off it in 2017.

entries.claim: Granger read the order from the balcony of Ashton Villa.
entries.detail: FOLKLORE, not evidence. No contemporaneous source places the reading there. Documented sites are the Union headquarters at the Osterman Building, the 1861 Custom House, the courthouse, and the "Negro Church" — today’s Reedy Chapel-AME. The belief is sustained by an annual Sons of Union Veterans reenactment performed AT Ashton Villa, a commemoration widely mistaken for the event it commemorates. The `era` clue asserted it as fact and the THEME BLURB asserted it flatly; both were rewritten.

sources.title: National Archives — General Order No. 3, the original document

replacement.clue: What ended in Galveston that June, and what began the next morning, which was harder.

entries.claim: The red drink descends from West African hibiscus and kola traditions.
entries.detail: WEAKLY SOURCED and widely repeated as fact. Opie, Miller and Twitty all hedge — "may come from", "some historians believe". There is plant provenance and colour symbolism, and no documentary chain. The shipped clue is already the safe version and claims no unbroken line. Keep it, and refuse any edit that hardens it.

sources.title: Britannica — Juneteenth

entries.claim: Texas made Juneteenth a state holiday in 1980, the first state to do so.
entries.detail: The shipped clue had Texas schools letting out for the day, which is unsourceable and probably false — Emancipation Day is a partial-staffing state-employee holiday and school years end before 19 June. The real fact is stronger anyway.

sources.title: Britannica — Juneteenth

replacement.clue: What Texas gave the day in 1980, first in the nation, when no calendar up north carried it.

entries.claim: HBCU enrollment is roughly 64% women, and has been women-majority every year since 1976.
entries.detail: NCES fall 2018: 142,108 women of 223,163 total — 63.7%, about 1:1.75. The premise two packs were authored on ("60%+") was conservative rather than wrong. No board needs changing.

sources.title: NCES — HBCU enrollment by sex

entries.claim: Xavier University of Louisiana is the only Catholic HBCU, founded by Katharine Drexel and the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament — NOT a Jesuit institution.
entries.detail: A whole shipped board was built on the false premise, with three errors at once: Xavier is not Jesuit (Loyola New Orleans is, and is not an HBCU); enrollment is 3,181 as of fall 2023, not "fifteen hundred"; and the board’s own second clue said "eight hundred", contradicting its first. No Jesuit institution is an HBCU, so the base word could not carry the board honestly however the clues were rewritten. Re-based to `priest`, with the correction itself now in the base clue.

sources.title: Xavier University of Louisiana — facts and figures

replacement.clue: New Orleans has a college downtown run by these men. The Catholic HBCU nearby was founded by nuns.

entries.claim: A 90s R&B group royalty ran around 56 cents per album, split among the members.
entries.detail: The shipped clue said "a penny a record" — off by roughly twentyfold. TLC’s 1991 LaFace deal paid 56c per album split three ways, about 19c each. The real number is more damning than the invented one, which is usually how this goes. [2026-08-11: the board carrying this clue was removed when the 90s pack was rebuilt vocabulary-first. Finding retained, citation cleared — it vouches for no live text.]

sources.title: TLC’s LaFace royalty terms, reported

replacement.clue: Fifty-six of them per album, split three ways, and the lawyers called that a deal.

entries.claim: Philadelphia’s soul studio of record is Sigma Sound, 212 N. 12th Street.
entries.detail: The shipped clue invented "three rooms over a Philadelphia subway grate" — evocative and resting on nothing. Sigma is the real room, and Joe Tarsia’s description of the Philly sound as Black music "in a tuxedo" is the better image. [2026-08-11: the board carrying this clue was removed when the 90s pack was rebuilt vocabulary-first. Finding retained, citation cleared — it vouches for no live text.]

sources.title: Sigma Sound Studios, 212 N. 12th St., Philadelphia

replacement.clue: Twelfth and Callowhill, where the city's soul got cut in a tuxedo for thirty years.

entries.claim: New jack swing was named in 1987, not the 1990s.
entries.detail: Barry Michael Cooper coined it in the Village Voice, 18 October 1987, writing about Teddy Riley. No shipped clue gets this wrong; recorded so none ever does.

sources.title: Barry Michael Cooper coins "new jack swing", Village Voice, 18 Oct 1987

entries.claim: Quiet storm is a radio format, originated by Melvin Lindsey at WHUR in May 1976 and named by Cathy Hughes.
entries.detail: Three shipped clues rest on this and all hold.

sources.title: WHUR — the Quiet Storm format, Melvin Lindsey, 1976

entries.claim: The Chicago stepping answer to a sticky floor is the shoe, not the floor.
entries.detail: The shipped clue had her shaking powder onto a sticky gym floor. Powdered dance-floor wax is a real product, but within the community powder is the crutch of dancers "who don’t pick up their feet", many studios forbid it, and the actual fix is leather or suede soles, brushed. The clue also contradicted the pack’s own `sole` clue, which is verified and correct.

sources.title: Cumbe Dance — Chicago Style Steppin’, sole guidance

replacement.clue: What a rubber sole leaves on a swept floor, and why nobody here wears one.

entries.claim: The spades pack never says "board" (the four-book minimum) or "set", and its two joker clues describe two different decks.
entries.detail: Terminology otherwise checks out against McIntyre: book, renege (three books or 100 points, challenger must prove it), blind bids gated on being 100 or 140 behind, game to 250/300/500, bags recorded beside the bid. The joker inconsistency is an authoring fix, not a research question — pick one deck.

sources.title: Amina McIntyre, on spades, American Journal of Play (2021)

entries.claim: Eyes on the Prize is 14 episodes across two series (1987, 1990); Series II was never commercially rights-cleared.
entries.detail: Roughly 130 songs licensed; PBS broadcast rights ended 1993 and licences lapsed by 1995, pushing VHS sets near $1,000 by 2005. Ford and Gilder funded re-clearance and Series I was restored in 2005. This is why the WashU interview outtakes — not the films — are the practical research door. Companion books are in copyright and are cited, never reproduced.

sources.title: Washington University — Henry Hampton Collection (Eyes on the Prize)

entries.claim: Baltimore "lake trout" is silver hake sold as whiting, and it is carryout culture, not a lodge basement.
entries.detail: The fish identification is confirmed by scientific name — it is neither lake nor trout. But the shipped clue put the phrase in a fraternal-lodge fish fry, and the word is the tell: lake trout belongs to a carryout counter. The replacement uses "whiting", accurate and right for the room, and keeps the joke.

sources.title: Baltimore Sun — what Baltimore "lake trout" actually is

replacement.clue: What the paper towels never quite do to your hands after breading forty pounds of whiting.

entries.claim: Chicago lakefront parking is metered and plate-read, not a permit on the dash; grilling is banned on the beaches and in Grant Park.
entries.detail: The shipped clue had a permit on the dash and a noon ticket sweep. Reality is ParkChicago meters and licence-plate-reading gates. Useful for authors: the Park District picnic permit threshold is 50 people and $45, and this board is a lakefront PARK scene, which is legal, rather than a beach one, which would not be. [2026-08-11: the board carrying this clue was removed when The Cookout was rebuilt vocabulary-first against the bench-signed vocabulary. Finding retained, citation cleared — it vouches for no live text, and a future cookout board about the lakefront should pick it back up.]

sources.title: Chicago Park District — picnic permits and lakefront rules

replacement.clue: What you take at the lakefront lot, where a camera reads your plate and bills you by the hour.

entries.claim: The regional food specifics across Fish Fry and The Cookout hold.
entries.detail: Milwaukee perch with rye and potato pancakes; Ohio Legion cod; New England haddock; Pittsburgh Knights of Columbus cod with pierogi and haluski; Big Bob Gibson, Decatur 1925, chickens dipped in white sauce AFTER smoking; Central Texas post oak with Big Red (Waco, 1937); eastern NC burn barrel and shovel; SoCal fire rings first-come except Huntington Beach. All three fish-fry institutional strands are documented — Black church fundraising best of the three, the VFW/Legion circuit least.

sources.title: Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q — Decatur, 1925, white sauce

entries.claim: "Front eye" for the front burner is real, living South/Appalachian usage.
entries.detail: Real but thinly citable: DARE is paywalled and no published food-writing instance was located. Keep the clue — the risk was that it reads as an ERROR to a non-Southern player, which is a tone question rather than a factual one. "Icebox" is generational rather than Southern- or Black-specific, and the packs never claim otherwise.

sources.title: Dictionary of American Regional English (paywalled)

entries.claim: The no-soap-on-cast-iron rule.
entries.detail: A non-finding, recorded so nobody re-opens it: the doctrine does not appear in these packs at all. The two cast-iron clues state the heat-dry and warm-oil steps, which Lodge and America’s Test Kitchen both endorse. For the record, soap does not strip polymerised seasoning — the rule dates to lye soap, and at least one state extension service still prints it as fact.

sources.title: Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q — Decatur, 1925, white sauce

entries.claim: Boyz II Men's "End of the Road" spent 13 consecutive weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1992, produced by L.A. Reid and Babyface with Daryl Simmons.
entries.detail: Released 30 June 1992; the 13th week at number one fell in the 7 November 1992 issue, the longest run in the chart's archive at that point. Broken the same year by Whitney Houston's 14 weeks with "I Will Always Love You" — so "the record" is only true for a few weeks, and no clue should claim it stood.

sources.title: Billboard, Rewinding the Charts: 1992
End of the Road (Boyz II Men song)

entries.claim: Brandy and Monica's "The Boy Is Mine" spent 13 weeks at number one in 1998 and was the year's best-selling US single.
entries.detail: Topped the Hot 100 dated 6 June 1998. Brandy was 19 and Monica 17. Produced by Rodney "Darkchild" Jerkins with Brandy and Dallas Austin; written by LaShawn Daniels, Rodney Jerkins, Fred Jerkins III, Japhe Tejada and Brandy Norwood. The "feud" framing is press narrative — clues should stay on the record, not the rivalry.

sources.title: Billboard, Brandy & Monica's The Boy Is Mine Was No. 1 In 1998
The Boy Is Mine (Brandy and Monica song)

entries.claim: Monica's "The First Night" reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1998 and held it for five weeks.
entries.detail: The drafted clue read "Monica's first, and she was fifteen" — wrong twice. "The First Night" is a 1998 release, when Monica was 18; her debut single was "Don't Take It Personal (Just One of Dem Days)" in 1995. The title word "first" invited the conflation, which is exactly how a clue turns into a false claim.

sources.title: The First Night
Stereogum, The Number Ones: Monica's The First Night

entries.replacement: Monica held number one five weeks with it, 1998

entries.claim: "Protect Ya Neck" was Wu-Tang Clan's debut single, self-released in December 1992 and re-released on Loud in May 1993.
entries.detail: The drafted clue dated it 1993. The independent Wu-Tang Records pressing was 14 December 1992; Loud re-released it 3 May 1993 with "Method Man" as the B-side, and it appeared on Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) on 9 November 1993. Produced by RZA, featuring eight of the nine original members — Masta Killa had not joined.

sources.title: Protect Ya Neck
Discogs, Wu-Tang Clan – Protect Ya Neck, 12" 1992

entries.replacement: Wu-Tang debut single, 1992, and the whole thing starts

entries.claim: "Gin and Juice" was the second single from Snoop Doggy Dogg's Doggystyle, released 18 January 1994; the album itself came out 23 November 1993.
entries.detail: Both drafted clues dated the song 1993, which is the ALBUM's year, not the single's. The distinction matters because the pack elsewhere dates singles, so a mixed convention would make the whole set unreliable.

sources.title: Gin and Juice
Doggystyle

entries.replacement: Snoop poured it with juice, single out January 1994
